newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Slim majority sees US rate hike Tuesday. [CORRECTED 13:55 GMT 24/9]
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Slim majority sees US rate hike Tuesday. [CORRECTED 13:55 GMT 24/9]

text.p: Signs of a robust U.S. economy will prompt the Federal Reserve to tighten short-term interest rates September 24, according to a narrow majority of economists in the latest Reuters international poll.
Eight of 15 experts surveyed in New York, London and Tokyo predicted a 25-basis-point hike in the Fed Funds rate at Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting.
Three of 15 economists said the Fed will next tighten at the FOMC meeting on November 13, while three others predicted the next move would be an easing some time in 1997.
The strength of the U.S. economy is unlikely to wane by year-end, said an official at Standard Chartered Bank in London who expects the Fed to hike interest rates on Tuesday.
"There is still reasonable momentum in the economy and we don't expect this to ease until next year," the official said.
"There is also a lag between economic activity and inflation, which the Fed will try to preempt," he added.
Experts in the Pacific Rim, however, said the outcome of Tuesday's FOMC meeting will be a tossup. They added that any move in short-term interest rates is likely to be modest.
"It's a 50/50 percent chance that the Fed would hike (the Fed Funds) rate at the upcoming FOMC," said Takumi Tsunoda, economist at Yamaichi Research Institute. (Corrects from "Nikko Research Center")
Even if the Fed raises the Fed Funds rate, the move will be small, Tsunoda said. "A 50 basis point hike in the discount rate and Fed Funds rate is very unlikely," he said.
"I think it's a close call," said John Ryding, senior economist at Bear, Stearns & Co Inc. Amid mixed signs on the economy, he said, FOMC members would exercise extra prudence.
"The case for not tightening is that core inflation pressures are completely absent," Ryding said.
He noted that "the Fed Funds rate is relatively high compared to the inflation rate," but added that a stronger economy than the Fed forecast support the case for tightening.

Further complicated the outlook, Ryding cited a Reuters report last Tuesday that 8 of 12 Fed district banks submitted requests for a hike in the discount rate. This suggests a great deal of pressure within the FOMC to raise rates, he said. Whether Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan goes along with the push for higher rates is an open question.
Ultimately, Greenspan's view of monetary policy will boil down to the current state of the U.S. economy, experts said.

William Brown, chief economist at J.P. Morgan Securities Inc, forecast a rate hike on Tuesday because "the economy has been substantially stronger than (the Fed) had anticipated when they eased policy earlier in the year."
"The unemployment rate has fallen and there are some signs of upward wage pressure," he added.
